title: Payroll — LinkedIn post bank
note: Personal-profile posts: copy and paste into LinkedIn, then post or use the native Schedule (clock) button. 3–4/week, mix segments.

posts.title: If you're the founder still doing payroll at 11pm, this one's for you
posts.cap:
There's a version of the small-business owner I meet a lot. Runs the company all day, then sits down after everyone's gone home to do the payroll — CPF, payslips, making sure everyone's paid right. At 11pm. Again.

If that's you: the real cost isn't the hour. It's that it's always on your mind.

Here's the cheap way out — and how to get your evenings back.
https://jte.com.sg/blog/founder-doing-payroll-late-night/

posts.title: You just won a 2-year project. Who runs payroll for 200 new hires?
posts.cap:
You win a 2-year project. Everyone's celebrating. Then it sinks in — you need to onboard and pay 200 people fast, and your HR team is still the same three folks it was last week.

I've sat with a lot of manufacturing and engineering bosses at exactly this moment. The work's won; the headache is payroll.

Wrote down how I'd actually handle it — including why we can run that payroll for almost nothing.
https://jte.com.sg/blog/project-staffing-payroll-singapore/

posts.title: What outsourcing payroll actually frees you up to do
posts.cap:
Everyone thinks outsourcing payroll is about saving admin hours. It's not really — that's the small part.

The bigger thing is what those hours were stopping you from doing: your HR stuck on CPF instead of real people work, you double-checking figures at night instead of running the business.

For a smaller company, that's the whole point. Wrote about it.
https://jte.com.sg/blog/what-outsourcing-payroll-frees-up/

posts.title: Why I give the first year of payroll free
posts.cap:
Every time I tell an employer we'll run their payroll free for the first year, the reaction is the same: a pause, then "okay, what's the catch?"

Fair question. If something sounds too good, people should be suspicious.

So I wrote the honest version — how it actually works, who's really paying, and why there's no catch for you.
https://jte.com.sg/blog/why-first-year-payroll-free/

posts.title: Why hiring temp HR for a project usually backfires
posts.cap:
When a project blows up your headcount, the first instinct is to hire temp HR. I get it. But I've watched it go sideways more often than not.

The admin an intern could do. The real coordination needs someone experienced — and experienced HR people don't want a 2-year contract. So you overpay, or you settle for less than you needed.

There's a cleaner way: hand the payroll out, keep your HR for the work that actually needs them.
https://jte.com.sg/blog/temp-hr-for-project-contract/

posts.title: The admin nobody warns you about when you become the boss
posts.cap:
When you start a business, everyone warns you about cashflow and customers. Nobody warns you about the admin.

The day you hire your first person, you quietly sign up for a second job you didn't apply for — CPF, payslips, filings, every month, on time, correctly.

It's not hard. It's just relentless. And you don't have to be the one doing it.
https://jte.com.sg/blog/admin-nobody-warns-new-boss/

posts.title: Setting up a sales office in Singapore? You don't need an HR team first
posts.cap:
If you're opening a sales or support office in Singapore, somewhere in the planning someone says "we'll need HR and payroll set up." Suddenly a lean little office looks like a big commitment.

You don't actually need all that to start. You can put two or three people on the ground here — properly employed, CPF and all — without setting up your own entity or building a back-office first.

Wrote down the lighter way to do it.
https://jte.com.sg/blog/sales-office-singapore-no-hr-team/

posts.title: When you should hire a real HR person (and when you shouldn't)
posts.cap:
I spend a lot of time telling people they don't need to hire HR just for payroll. So let me say the other half out loud: sometimes you absolutely should.

A good HR person is for the people side — hiring, progression, keeping good staff. That's worth every cent.

But if the real reason you're hiring one is payroll eating your time? That's an admin problem, not a people one. Here's the honest line between the two.
https://jte.com.sg/blog/when-to-hire-real-hr-singapore/

posts.title: How to scale headcount for a project without burning out your HR
posts.cap:
There's a kind of growth that quietly breaks HR teams — the project spike. 50 staff to 300 in a few weeks because a contract demands it, then back down when it ends.

You can't solve something temporary with permanent hires. And onboarding 300 people correctly, fast, is a mountain most HR teams aren't sized for.

Here's how I'd take the heaviest part off their plate.
https://jte.com.sg/blog/scaling-headcount-project-hiring-singapore/

posts.title: Growing from 5 to 20 staff? This is when payroll gets real
posts.cap:
There's a size where a business quietly changes character — somewhere around 5 to 20 staff. Below five, payroll fits in your head. Past twenty, you've got structure. The messy bit is in between.

It's the stretch where doing payroll yourself stops working: the edge cases pile up, and a slip with CPF is the expensive kind.

Here's how to get ahead of it before it bites.
https://jte.com.sg/blog/growing-5-to-20-staff-payroll/

posts.title: Contract manufacturers and logistics: the payroll move that saves your HR
posts.cap:
If you run on contracts — manufacturing, logistics, engineering — your headcount is never still. People ramp on for a project, roll off when it ends, and your HR team is always onboarding or offboarding someone.

A fixed, permanent HR cost is an awkward fit for a business that moves like that.

Wrote about a payroll setup that flexes with your contracts instead — and costs almost nothing.
https://jte.com.sg/blog/contract-manufacturing-logistics-payroll/

posts.title: A few things handling payroll for other companies taught me
posts.cap:
I've handled payroll and onboarding for a lot of companies over the years. After a while you stop seeing individual companies and start seeing patterns.

Nobody enjoys doing payroll. The person stuck with it usually wears five hats. And the mistakes stay quiet — until they're loud.

Wrote down what it all taught me.
https://jte.com.sg/blog/lessons-handling-payroll-singapore/
